newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-NORMAN SHARES LEAD BUT MONTY AND BAKER-FINCH CRASH.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-NORMAN SHARES LEAD BUT MONTY AND BAKER-FINCH CRASH.

text.p: Australian Greg Norman and Americans Fred Couples and Justin Leonard survived Royal Troon's vicious back nine and a strong wind to shoot two-under-par 69s for the early first round lead in the British Open on Thursday.
Norman, the 1986 and 1993 champion, and Couples, winner of the 1992 Masters, did what they needed to do by making hay on the front nine and then limiting the damage coming back into the wind.
Leonard did it the hard way, two under for the front and then level par 35 on the back.
But local favourite Colin Montgomerie, who has missed four of the last five British Open cuts, went to pieces on the course where he played as a boy.
The U.S. Open runner-up could not stop blocking his tee shots to the right and hit only the first three fairways in a disappointing five-over-par 76.
But worse was to come from ex-Open champion Ian Baker-Finch who slumped to a disastrous 92, 21-over.
Norman played the front nine in four-under 32 and the back in two-over 37 while Couples, whose father is seriously ill with leukaemia, shot 31-38 for his 69.
"We are playing two different golf courses out there," said Norman, who dropped shots at the 13th and the last. "The wind is heavy and it is very cold. Coming home you have to hang on.
"You can hit good shots and feel like a fool. I hit 37 shots on the back nine and 15 of them I never ever practise.

"We have not had enough wind in recent British Opens and you really have to work at it. I'm delighted with my score and a lot of guys would like to have it but there are three more hard days to go," he said.
Norman birdied the third and fourth holes, dropped a shot at the fifth but then collected further birdies at the sixth, seventh and ninth.
Couples, having a poor year with his recurring bad back, has been concerned for the health of his father after he recently required a course of chemotherapy for his illness.
"He's always been very fit but he has lost a lot of weight. He has started to put it back on now," Couples said.
"My back is okay right now but I need to see my coach. I would very much like to win another major title," he said.
"I made a couple of bombs but it would have been nice to make the five-footer on 18," he said after holing putts of 20, 15 and 12 feet to save pars on the back nine.
His dropped shots came at the 10th and 11th, where the wind changes direction from the front nine, and the last where he missed the green and missed the five-footer.
Angel Cabrera of Argentina was a shot behind the leaders on 70 with five-times winner Tom Watson on 71, level with Ian Woosnam of Britain.
Cabrera, 27, is Argentina's best player on the European Tour now and was delighted with his putting in his first British Open round.
"I think I had under 30 putts," he said. "But I play better on normal courses."
Watson did not hit any greens in regulation figures in his back nine of 38 but chipped well to limit the damage.
"I didn't put myself out of play. That's what you have to do on this golf course.
"This is nothing new. Everybody knows what the wind is like. The back nine is one of the toughest nines in golf."
"It was like playing the Chicago Bulls. You know they're going to come back at you at the end so you better get a pretty big lead," Watson added.
Montgomerie, winner of the Irish Open after a closing 62 this month, looked a little shell-shocked after his 76.
"I've done badly in British Opens before. Whether I do well tomorrow or not, I'll come back from this and it won't hurt," he said.
"I just kept pushing shots. It wasn't the wind particularly.
"The back nine is very playable if I hit the fairways and hit my iron shots good enough.
"Provided I hit the fairways tomorrow I can birdie any hole and I am still confident of doing that," the big Scot, still searching for his first major title, said.

However, Montgomery's troubles paled alongside those of Baker-Finch. The winner of the 1991 Open had a nightmare day, firing 21-over par in a round described by one observer as the "saddest thing I've ever seen on a golf course."
The Australian has struggled amid injury to find any sort of form in recent years and earlier this week said he was going to pull out of the Open rather than play a poor round.
